# Public debt and government bonds (`public_debt_bonds`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/economy.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Economy & finance (`economy`)
- Deps: helped by banking_credit, double_entry, representative_government, stock_exchange
- Core idea: The state borrows from many lenders at once by issuing standard, transferable bonds that pay a fixed interest, with specific taxes pledged to pay it and ideally an assembly of taxpayers and lenders that has voted the debt. Because a holder can sell his bond to someone else, he does not need to wait for repayment, so he accepts a lower rate; perpetual bonds need never be repaid at all. A state that always pays can spread the cost of a war over decades instead of debasing coin or seizing property. Minimum design: earmarked revenue, an office independent of the ruler that collects it and pays the interest, a public register of holders, and an unbroken record of paying on time.
- Pitfalls:
  - Treating a royal loan from a banker as public debt: kings who could default at will paid far higher rates than city-republics whose creditors governed
  - Borrowing without a pledged revenue: lenders stop lending and the state defaults (Spain under Philip II repeatedly)
  - Forced loans or arbitrary cuts in interest destroy the market for decades
  - Assuming all debt is ruin: Britain carried a debt above twice its yearly income after 1815 and prospered, because it paid reliably
  - Inflating the debt away works once; afterwards lenders demand much higher rates
- History: greece: 4th c. BC – Greek cities borrow from temple treasuries (Delos) and from citizens for specific needs; rome: Republic – loans from citizens in emergencies (210 BC), repaid in instalments; the Empire avoided long-term debt; china: imperial China rarely borrowed, financing by taxes and paper money; 1894–1898 first domestic bond issues, foreign loans after 1860s; islamic: 1775 – Ottoman esham, tradeable life shares in tax revenues; 1854 first foreign loan; 1875 default and 1881 Ottoman Public Debt Administration; europe: 1262 – Venice consolidates forced loans into the Monte Vecchio, 5 % transferable claims; 1345 Florence's Monte Comune; 1407 Genoa's Casa di San Giorgio; 1522 Paris rentes; 1540s Holland's province bonds; 1693–1694 English national debt and Bank of England; 1751 consols; americas: 1790 – Hamilton funds the US federal debt and assumes the states' debts
- Read:
  - P. G. M. Dickson, The Financial Revolution in England (1967)
  - Douglass C. North & Barry R. Weingast, Constitutions and Commitment, Journal of Economic History 49 (1989)
  - James D. Tracy, A Financial Revolution in the Habsburg Netherlands (1985)
